tips.title: Extension, not length
tips.body: $F = ke$ uses the **extension**: the new length **minus** the original. Putting the whole length in is the most common error in the topic, and it makes $k$ come out far too small.

tips.title: Metres, not centimetres
tips.body: A spring constant is in N/m, so convert the extension before dividing. Leaving it in centimetres makes $k$ a hundred times too small and is easy to miss.

tips.title: The limit of proportionality
tips.body: The graph is a straight line through the origin **until** the limit of proportionality. Past it the line curves and $F = ke$ no longer holds. A question about a curved section is usually testing that.

tips.title: Convert the units before the maths
tips.body: Change every length to **metres** and every force to **newtons** as the first line of working. Doing the conversion once, at the start, keeps $k$ in N/m and stops the hundredfold error that comes from noticing centimetres only after the division.

steps.title: Stretching, compressing, bending
steps.body:
To change the shape of an object you need **more than one force**. A single force would just move it. Pull both ends of a spring and it stretches; push both ends and it compresses.

If the object returns to its original shape when the forces are removed, the deformation was **elastic**. If it stays deformed, it was **inelastic**.

visuals.alt: Four identical springs hanging from a bar with loads of 0, 1, 2 and 3 newtons, extending by 4, 8 and 12 centimetres

check.prompt: A metal ruler is bent slightly and springs back. Which is true?
check.solution: It returned to its original shape: elastic.
options: Only one force acted on it

steps.title: Hooke's law: force is proportional to extension
steps.body:
Double the force and the spring extends twice as far. In symbols:

$$F = k e$$

$F$ is the force in newtons, $e$ is the **extension** in metres (the extra length, not the whole length), and $k$ is the **spring constant** in newtons per metre. A stiff spring has a large $k$. The same equation works for compression.

check.prompt: A spring has $k = 25$ N/m. What force, in newtons, gives an extension of 0.08 m?

steps.title: Finding the spring constant
steps.body: Convert centimetres to metres before anything else. It is the step examiners see slip most often.

visuals.problem: A 6 N force extends a spring by 12 cm. Find $k$.

check.prompt: A 4 N force extends a spring by 8 cm. Find $k$ in N/m.
check.skill: finding k with a unit conversion

steps.title: The force–extension graph
steps.body: Force on the $y$-axis, extension on the $x$-axis. While Hooke's law holds the graph is a **straight line through the origin** and its **gradient is $k$**. At the **limit of proportionality** the line starts to curve: extension grows faster than force. Up to the limit of proportionality the relationship between force and extension is **linear**; beyond it, it is **non-linear**. The spring may still be elastic for a while beyond that, and eventually it deforms permanently.

visuals.alt: Force in newtons on the vertical axis against extension in metres on the horizontal axis: a straight line through the origin with gradient 50 newtons per metre, marked at (0.1, 5). The graph shows only the proportional part, up to the limit of proportionality

steps.text: Straight section: force ÷ extension is constant, and that constant is $k$
The point where the line first bends away is the limit of proportionality
Beyond it the same extra force gives a bigger extension, so the graph curves towards the extension axis
Take $k$ only from the straight part, using a large triangle

check.prompt: What does the gradient of a force–extension graph represent?

steps.title: Required practical: force and extension
steps.body:
Hang the spring from a clamp stand with a metre rule beside it. Record the unstretched length. Add masses one at a time and record the new length; extension is the difference. Convert mass to force with $W = mg$.

**Independent** variable: force. **Dependent**: extension. **Control**: the same spring throughout. Read the ruler at eye level to avoid parallax. If the plotted points start to curve away from the straight line, the spring has passed its limit of proportionality, and only the straight part should be used for the gradient.

steps.text: Extension $=$ stretched length $-$ original length, in metres

check.prompt: Which is the independent variable in this practical?
check.solution: You choose and change the force; the extension responds.

steps.title: Energy stored in a stretched spring
steps.body:
Stretching a spring does work on it, and that work is stored in the **elastic potential** store:

$$E_e = \tfrac{1}{2} k e^2$$

Only while the spring obeys Hooke's law. Square the extension, in metres, before multiplying.

check.prompt: A spring with $k = 100$ N/m is extended by 0.2 m. Calculate the elastic potential energy in joules.

steps.title: Your turn: read the graph
steps.body: Drag the extension and watch the force. The line is straight because $F = ke$; its steepness is $k$.

visuals.fallback: A straight line from the origin: 2.5 N at 0.05 m, 5 N at 0.1 m, 10 N at 0.2 m, so the spring constant is 50 N/m.

check.prompt: On the graph, what is the spring constant in N/m?
check.solution: Force $\div$ extension at any point: $5 \div 0.1 = 50$ N/m.

steps.title: Going deeper: area under the graph, and weight from mass
steps.body:
The **area under** a force–extension graph is the work done stretching the spring. For the straight part that area is a triangle, $\tfrac{1}{2} F e$, and since $F = ke$ it equals $\tfrac{1}{2} k e^2$: the two equations are the same fact. Beyond the limit of proportionality the area under the curve still gives the work done. Past the **elastic limit**, a little further on, the spring deforms permanently and some of that energy goes to the thermal store instead of being stored elastically.

Top questions also give a **mass** rather than a force. Convert with $W = mg$, $g = 9.8$ N/kg, and mind the grams.

visuals.problem: 300 g mass on a spring with $k = 40$ N/m

steps.text: $e = \dfrac{2.94}{40} = 0.0735$ m, which is 7.35 cm, about 7.4 cm

check.prompt: A spring with $k = 40$ N/m is extended by 0.15 m. Work out the area under its force–extension graph up to that point, in joules.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Deforming needs more than one force. Elastic returns; inelastic does not.
- $F = ke$: force in N, extension in m, $k$ in N/m. Convert cm to m first.
- Graph: straight through the origin, gradient $k$, curving past the limit of proportionality.
- $E_e = \tfrac{1}{2} k e^2$, the area under the straight part.
- Given a mass, find the weight with $W = mg$ before anything else.

visuals.alt: Three springs showing extension proportional to load: 1 newton gives 4 centimetres, 2 gives 8, 3 gives 12

A spring is stretched and returns to its original length when the force is removed. Which term describes this?
questions.solution: Elastic means it goes back. Inelastic or plastic means it stays stretched.

questions.skill: finding k with a unit conversion

questions.prompt: A spring with spring constant 15 N/m is pulled with a force of 3 N. Calculate its extension in metres.
On a force–extension graph, what happens beyond the limit of proportionality?
questions.solution: Past the limit the relationship is no longer linear. The spring may still deform, but not in proportion.
options: The spring snaps straight away, so the line stops at that point
The line stops being straight: extension grows faster than force
The extension stops increasing however much more force is added
The line becomes steeper and straighter as the spring stiffens

questions.prompt: A spring with spring constant 200 N/m is extended by 5 cm. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored, in joules.
In the required practical on force and extension, which is a control variable?
questions.solution: The spring stays the same throughout. Mass is changed (independent), extension is measured (dependent).

questions.prompt: A 400 g mass is hung from a spring with spring constant 49 N/m. Taking $g = 9.8$ N/kg, calculate the extension in cm.

A spring extends by 6 cm when a force of 3 N is applied. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored when the same spring is extended by 10 cm, assuming it stays within its limit of proportionality.
Describe how you would determine the spring constant of a spring by experiment, and explain how the graph you draw shows whether the spring has gone past its limit of proportionality.
questions.solution: Level-marked. Level 3 needs a method someone could follow, the graph, the gradient, and the curve past the limit.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points about the method, graph, gradient, and limit of proportionality, not linked
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a mostly correct account of the method, graph, gradient, and limit of proportionality with some links between points
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, complete account of the method, graph, gradient, and limit of proportionality with every step linked and correct physics terms

criteria.text: Equipment: clamp stand, spring, slotted masses, metre rule; measure the unstretched length first
Add known masses one at a time and measure the new length each time; extension = new length minus original
Convert mass to weight with $W = mg$ and repeat readings, reading at eye level to avoid parallax
Plot force on the $y$-axis against extension on the $x$-axis and draw a line of best fit
Spring constant is the gradient of the straight part of the line
The limit of proportionality is where the line stops being straight through the origin; beyond it the points curve away

questions.modelAnswer: Hang the spring from a clamp stand with a metre rule alongside and record its unstretched length. Add slotted masses one at a time, recording the new length each time; extension is the new length minus the original. Convert each mass to a force using $W = mg$. Read the ruler at eye level to avoid parallax, and repeat each reading. Plot force against extension and draw a line of best fit. The gradient of the straight section is the spring constant. If the later points curve away from the straight line, the spring has passed its limit of proportionality, and only the straight part should be used for the gradient.

questions.prompt: The graph shows force against extension for a spring up to an extension of 0.16 m. Use the gradient to determine the force needed for an extension of 0.2 m, assuming the spring is still within its limit of proportionality.

markScheme.description: Gradient found from two well-separated points

visual.alt: Force in newtons on the vertical axis against extension in metres on the horizontal axis: a straight line through the origin with two points marked and labelled, (0.04, 2) and (0.12, 6)

questions.prompt: A car suspension spring is compressed by 4 cm when a 1000 N load is placed on it. Calculate its spring constant in N/m.
questions.skill: spring constant of a compressed spring
questions.solution: Compression follows the same law as extension. $4$ cm $= 0.04$ m. $k = \dfrac{F}{e} = \dfrac{1000}{0.04} = 25\,000$ N/m.

questions.prompt: A newton meter is to be made from a spring with spring constant 250 N/m. Tests show its limit of proportionality is reached at an extension of 6 cm. Evaluate whether the spring is suitable for a newton meter that must read up to 20 N.
questions.solution: The calculation is one mark; the evaluation is the comparison, the judgement, and the improvement.

markScheme.description: Compared with 20 N with a reason
An improvement: stiffer spring, higher limit, or lower rating

criteria.text: 15 N is less than 20 N, so readings above 15 N would not be proportional and the scale would be wrong
Conclusion: not suitable as it stands
A fix: use a stiffer spring (higher $k$) or one with a higher limit, or restrict the meter to 15 N

questions.modelAnswer: At the limit of proportionality the force is $F = ke = 250 \times 0.06 = 15$ N. The meter must read to 20 N, and beyond 15 N the extension is no longer proportional to force, so the scale would read incorrectly and the spring might not return to its original length. The spring is not suitable. A spring with a higher spring constant, or a higher limit of proportionality, would be needed, or the meter should be rated to 15 N.

questions.prompt: A spring stores 0.5 J of elastic potential energy when it is extended by 10 cm. Calculate its spring constant in N/m.

markScheme.description: 10 cm converted to 0.1 m and squared

questions.prompt: A student hangs masses on a spring of unstretched length 4.0 cm and records the total length: 100 g gives 6.0 cm, 200 g gives 8.0 cm, 300 g gives 10.0 cm, 400 g gives 12.5 cm. Taking $g = 9.8$ N/kg, use the straight part of the results to calculate the spring constant, in N/m.
questions.solution: Extensions are 2.0, 4.0, 6.0 and 8.5 cm. The first three are proportional to the weights 0.98, 1.96 and 2.94 N, so they are on the straight part; the 400 g point is past the limit of proportionality and is left out. $k = \dfrac{2.94}{0.06} = 49$ N/m.

markScheme.description: Extension = total length − 4.0 cm, converted to metres
400 g result excluded as beyond the limit of proportionality

examTechnique.body: Under AQA's normal rules $F = ke$ is an equation you must recall, while $E_e = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^2$ is printed on the equation sheet. For the 2025 to 2027 exams AQA gave a full sheet with every equation on it; whether that continues for 2028 had not been confirmed when this was written, so learn both. Knowing them matters even with a sheet: it will not tell you which one the question needs, rearrange it for you, or convert your centimetres. The marks are for choosing, rearranging, converting units, and the final unit. This topic also carries a required practical, which can appear as a six-mark method question or as data to process.
examinerErrors: Using the whole length of the spring instead of the extension.
Forgetting to convert centimetres to metres, giving $k$ one hundred times too small.
Squaring $ke$ instead of $e$ in the energy equation.
Using mass in place of weight: 200 g is 0.2 kg, and its weight is 0.2 × 9.8 = 1.96 N, not 200 N and not 0.2 N.
Reading $k$ from a curved part of the graph.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer converts units before substituting, rearranges in symbols, uses the gradient of the straight section only, links the area under the graph to the energy equation, and describes the practical as variables, method, and processing rather than a story.
